newsitem.title: SAUDI ARABIA: Saudi firm to build private desalination plant.
newsitem.headline: Saudi firm to build private desalination plant.

text.p: A Saudi Arabian company plans to build the kingdom's first private water desalination plant at a cost of $50 million, the company's general manager said in remarks published on Sunday.

Saleh Hefni, Saudi Industrial Services Co (SISCO) general manager, told the English-language Arab News daily the 190 million riyal ($50 million) plant in the Red Sea city of Jeddah would start production in about two years. It would provide water to factories and industrial installations.
"We hope to start production by September 1999 and in the initial phase the plant will produce 20,000 cubic metres of desalinated water per day," Hefni said.
Arab News said the plant would be the first such private project in Saudi Arabia where the government has built 23 desalination plants producing 520 million gallons daily.
The government plans to increase the desalination capacity to 800 million gallons when water projects now being carried out under the 1995-2000 development plan are completed, it said.
SISCO is trying to secure a loan from the Saudi Industrial Development Fund to finance the first phase of the project.

Urban and industrial water consumption in Saudi Arabia is estimated at three billion cubic metres a year, which experts at a conference in the kingdom last week said could be cut by 25 percent if resources and supply networks were properly used.
Consumption could be trimmed by 50 percent if additional investments were made in the sector, they said.
But farming consumed the most water in the desert kingdom.

"The agricultural sector consumed 8.26 billion cubic metres per year according to estimates by the Ministry of Agriculture and Water or 14 billion cubic metres based on figures by the Ministry of Planning," the newspaper said.
Saudi Arabia depends on scarce rainfall, non-renewable underground water and desalination to supply water for its 18 million population, which is growing at three to four percent.
The government has already taken steps, such as a decision a year ago to stop grain exports, to drastically reduce water use.
